Centralized Error Handling →

Error-Handling Middleware

The four-argument function signature Express treats as a special case.

Ordinary middleware takes (req, res, next) — three arguments. Error-handling middleware takes four: (err, req, res, next). That extra leading argument isn't just a convention; Express literally counts a middleware function's argument count to decide whether it's a normal handler or an error handler. Four arguments, and Express only ever calls it when something upstream called next(err) — exactly what asyncHandler does (previous slide).

Figure 1.10 is this project's one error handler:

// Figure 1.10: turning an error into a response (src/middleware/errorHandler.js)
export default (err, req, res, next) => {
  const status = err.status || 500;

  res.status(status).json({
    error: { message: err.message || 'Internal Server Error' },
  });
};

err.status || 500 reads a status property off the error if one was set (none of this project's code sets one yet — that arrives with more deliberate error objects in Week 3), defaulting to 500 (Internal Server Error) otherwise. Same idea for the message, defaulting to a generic one so nothing ever ships an undefined message to a client.

Notice this function never calls next() itself — it's the end of the line. It doesn't need to, because sending a response (res.status(...).json(...)) is itself how a middleware chain ends; next() is only for continuing the chain.
